# Introduction

Forecasting tools can make it easy to generate predictions, but understanding how they work helps us decide when to rely on them. Different workloads have different patterns, and a model that works well for one may be less useful for another. In this post, I'll explore two forecasting approaches in R and test how well they predict phone volume.

Accurate phone forecasts can help teams balance phone coverage with other work and plan time for training, staff meetings, or system updates. Here, I'll use hourly counts of recorded inquiries to New York City's 311 call center to explore daily, weekly, and yearly patterns and test predictions against later observations.

I'll start with Prophet, which models trends and recurring patterns and can incorporate holidays or other predictors. Then I'll explore ETS (Error, Trend, Seasonality), an exponential smoothing approach that gives more weight to recent observations. I'll compare their predictions against actual call volumes and finish with a recommendation for this dataset, including the limitations of that comparison.

# Set-up

Before building the forecasts, I'll load the packages and bring in the data we'll use throughout the analysis.

I'll use tidyverse and lubridate to prepare the data, httr2 to download it, Prophet and ETS to forecast volume, and plotly for interactive charts.

```{r setup}
#| eval: true
#| code-fold: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(httr2)
library(prophet)
library(forecast)
library(plotly)
```

The [NYC 311 Call Center Inquiry dataset](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/311-Call-Center-Inquiry/wewp-mm3p/about_data) records agent-handled inquiries. I'll download hourly counts for 2015–2018, using the first three years for training and 2018 for testing. These counts exclude abandoned calls, and missing hours may not mean zero activity. This period also avoids pandemic-related underreporting beginning in March 2020.

```{r data}
#| eval: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

response <- request("https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/wewp-mm3p.csv") |>
  req_url_query(
    `$select` = "date_trunc_ymd(date_time) AS date, date_extract_hh(date_time) AS hour, count(*) AS inquiry_count",
    `$where` = "date_time >= '2015-01-01T00:00:00' AND date_time < '2019-01-01T00:00:00'",
    `$group` = "date,hour",
    `$order` = "date,hour",
    `$limit` = 100000
  ) |>
  req_timeout(180) |>
  req_perform()

data <- read_csv(I(resp_body_string(response)), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(date = as_date(date))
```

# Explore and Prepare the Data

Before fitting either model, I'll check the coverage and look for patterns in recorded inquiries. I'll focus on Monday–Friday to reflect a weekday phone operation. For now, each daily total includes all hours; narrowing the analysis to business hours will require a specific time window. The exploration uses 2015–2017, leaving 2018 aside for testing.

## Check Coverage

The download has one row per recorded date and hour. I'll check for duplicate rows and invalid values, then compare it with the expected hours for Monday–Friday. Missing hours stay missing rather than becoming zeros.

```{r check-coverage}
#| eval: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"

stopifnot(
  nrow(data) > 0,
  !anyNA(data),
  !anyDuplicated(data[c("date", "hour")]),
  all(data$hour %in% 0:23),
  all(data$inquiry_count >= 0)
)

hourly <- expand_grid(
  date = seq(as.Date("2015-01-01"), as.Date("2018-12-31"), by = "day"),
  hour = 0:23
) |>
  filter(wday(date, week_start = 1) <= 5) |>
  left_join(data, by = c("date", "hour"))

coverage <- hourly |>
  group_by(year = year(date)) |>
  summarise(
    expected_hours = n(),
    recorded_hours = sum(!is.na(inquiry_count)),
    missing_hours = sum(is.na(inquiry_count)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(coverage, col.names = c(
  "Year", "Expected hours", "Recorded hours", "Missing hours"
))
```

A missing hour could reflect no inquiries or a reporting gap. This check also flags calendar quirks such as daylight saving time. Any gaps need review before modeling; I won't assume an incomplete day's total represents a full day.

## Daily Volume

I'll total each day's inquiries, keeping incomplete days as missing. The first chart shows changes over time and any unusually high or low days worth investigating.

```{r daily-volume}
#| eval: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"

daily <- hourly |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(
    missing_hours = sum(is.na(inquiry_count)),
    inquiry_count = if (anyNA(inquiry_count)) NA_real_ else sum(inquiry_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

train <- daily |> filter(date < as.Date("2018-01-01"))
test <- daily |> filter(date >= as.Date("2018-01-01"))

daily_plot <- ggplot(train, aes(date, inquiry_count)) +
  geom_line(color = "#355C7D", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekday NYC 311 Inquiries, 2015–2017",
    x = NULL, y = "Recorded inquiries"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(daily_plot)
```

## Weekly and Yearly Patterns

Next, I'll compare average daily volume by weekday and by month within each year. Averages make the monthly comparison less sensitive to the number of days in each month. Both summaries exclude incomplete days.

```{r weekly-pattern}
#| eval: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"

weekly_pattern <- train |>
  filter(!is.na(inquiry_count)) |>
  mutate(weekday = wday(date, label = TRUE, week_start = 1) |> droplevels()) |>
  group_by(weekday) |>
  summarise(avg_inquiries = mean(inquiry_count), .groups = "drop")

weekly_plot <- ggplot(weekly_pattern, aes(weekday, avg_inquiries)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#355C7D") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Daily Inquiries by Weekday",
    x = NULL, y = "Average recorded inquiries"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(weekly_plot)
```

```{r yearly-pattern}
#| eval: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"

monthly_pattern <- train |>
  filter(!is.na(inquiry_count)) |>
  mutate(year = factor(year(date)), month = month(date, label = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(year, month) |>
  summarise(avg_inquiries = mean(inquiry_count), .groups = "drop")

monthly_plot <- ggplot(
  monthly_pattern, aes(month, avg_inquiries, color = year, group = year)
) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Weekday Inquiries by Month and Year",
    x = NULL, y = "Average recorded inquiries", color = "Year"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(monthly_plot)
```

I'll look for weekday differences, recurring monthly peaks, and changes in the overall level. These plots can suggest seasonal patterns, but three years of history provide only three observations of each annual cycle.

## Prepare for Modeling

Both models will use the same daily training data from 2015–2017 and be evaluated against 2018. I'll resolve any missing days before fitting them. Using daily totals preserves weekly patterns, though it won't tell us how many people are needed during individual hours.

```{r check-model-inputs}
#| code-summary: "Show Code"

# Pause modeling if any daily totals still need review.
stopifnot(!anyNA(train$inquiry_count), !anyNA(test$inquiry_count))
```

# Prophet

```{r}
# model data
model_prophet <- prophet(
  prophet_payment,
  weekly.seasonality = FALSE,
  daily.seasonality = FALSE
)
# forecast the next 12 month
future <- make_future_dataframe(
  model_prophet,
  periods = 12,
  freq = "month"
)
# generate forecast
forecast <- predict(model_prophet, future)
# plot
plot(model_prophet, forecast) |>
  ggplotly()
```


```{r}
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-width: 8
# modify data
forecast_yoy <- forecast |>
  select(ds, yhat, yhat_lower, yhat_upper) |>
  left_join(prophet_payment, by = "ds") |>
  mutate(
    `Calls Offered` = if_else(is.na(y), yhat, y),
    type = if_else(is.na(y), "Forecast", "Actual"),
    year = year(ds),
    month = month(ds, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)
  )
# plot 
forecast_yoy |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = `Calls Offered`, fill = type)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(`Calls Offered`)), vjust = -0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ year, ncol = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title = "Payment Calls Offered Forecast by Month",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Calls Offered",
    fill = NULL
  ) 
```
